evidence: src/application/ports.ts declares only the IdGenerator.next() and Clock.now() ports, which ProjectService, TaskService and UserService inject through their constructors.
src/application/project-service.ts ProjectService.create delegates to the domain createProject(this.ids.next(), name, this.clock.now()) and persists the result through ProjectRepository.save.

src/application/task-service.ts TaskService.markDone delegates the state change to task.markDone(this.clock.now()), and assign delegates to task.assignTo(userId), so the task rules stay in the domain.
src/application/user-service.ts UserService.register delegates to the domain createUser(this.ids.next(), name).

Minor overlap: TaskService.requireProject in src/application/task-service.ts and ProjectService.get in src/application/project-service.ts both throw NotFoundError("Project", id) after projects.findById. This is a trivial lookup, not a duplicated invariant.
parsedVerdict.reasoning: The src/application module is one cohesive use-case layer. ports.ts declares the IdGenerator and Clock ports. ProjectService, TaskService and UserService each wrap one domain aggregate. All three get ids and time through the injected ports (this.ids.next(), this.clock.now()), so they use the module's abstractions consistently and never call system time or random directly. Creating and changing domain objects is left to the domain (createProject, createUser, new Task, task.assignTo, task.markDone), so the services do not re-implement business invariants. The only overlap is that TaskService.requireProject repeats the project-lookup check of ProjectService.get, throwing NotFoundError("Project", id). This is a trivial existence check on a shared repository port, not a duplicated business invariant, and services depending on repositories directly is the normal pattern here, not a bypass. TaskService.requireUser serves a different purpose: it validates the assignee and throws ValidationError, unlike UserService.get. Overall the unit meets the rubric.
